Ijachi, an attacking midfielder and defender from Mavlon FC in Lagos, emerged as Nigeria’s standout performer, scoring 11 goals and providing three assists during the festival, which runs from 22 to 31 October.
The teenager’s goal-scoring exploits, leadership and ability to influence matches have placed him among the Nigerian youngsters to watch as the country seeks to develop a new generation capable of representing the senior national team, the Super Eagles, in the years ahead.
While the festival provides a platform for young players to gain international exposure and experience, Ijachi’s return of 11 goals and three assists offers an encouraging indication of his attacking potential.
His performances also underline the importance of sustained investment in youth development, particularly in identifying, nurturing and exposing promising players to competitive football beyond Nigeria’s domestic academy system.
The maiden FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival brings together young footballers in an international environment designed to provide competitive experience and opportunities for development at an early stage of their careers.
For Nigeria, the performances of Ijachi and his teammates have provided a glimpse of the talent emerging from the country’s grassroots football system.
Ijachi’s tournament was highlighted by a superb hat-trick in Nigeria’s emphatic 7–0 victory over New Caledonia, a performance that demonstrated his ability to convert attacking opportunities and influence a match decisively.
The Mavlon FC youngster also scored the winning goal in a 2–1 comeback victory over Cyprus, underlining his importance when the team needed a decisive contribution.
His scoring record extended to a brace against Benin in a 6–3 defeat and another two-goal performance against Jordan in a 2–2 draw.
Those contributions demonstrated his ability to find the net in different match situations, from a dominant victory to tightly contested encounters in which individual moments can determine the outcome.
The Nigerian captain also continued to contribute despite playing through a knock sustained earlier in the tournament against The Gambia, in a match that ended 3–3.
His willingness to remain involved despite the setback added another dimension to his tournament performance, although his fitness and long-term development will require careful management as he continues his football journey.
Beyond his goals, Ijachi’s role as captain has placed him at the centre of the Future Eagles’ efforts, with his responsibilities extending to leadership and involvement in the team’s attacking play.
For a player operating in midfield and also capable of defensive duties, his goal return is particularly noteworthy.
However, while the statistics make a strong case for his emergence as one of the tournament’s most productive Nigerian players, his future progress will depend on continued technical development, tactical understanding, physical conditioning and exposure to increasingly demanding competition.
While Ijachi has attracted the headlines, other members of the Future Eagles squad have also provided encouraging signs of their potential at the Baku festival.
Wisdom Oche, a forward from Shakhandam Academy in Abuja, made an early contribution to Nigeria’s scoring efforts and found the net against Cyprus and New Caledonia.
Oche’s attacking involvement gives the coaching and development teams another player to monitor as they assess the squad’s potential beyond the immediate tournament.
Abdulsalam Muhammad of Simonben Academy in Kaduna also contributed goals during Nigeria’s 7–0 demolition of New Caledonia.
His performance in that commanding victory highlighted the contribution of players beyond the team captain, suggesting that Nigeria’s attacking threat is not dependent on a single individual.
Wisdom Boniface, a forward from Adoration Academy, which has links to Enugu and Abuja, also made his mark by scoring during the encounter against Benin.
Although Nigeria lost that match 6–3, Boniface’s contribution offered a positive individual moment in a contest that exposed the team to the demands of a high-scoring international encounter.
Mayowa Salu, who is part of the Nigeria Football Federation’s Talent Development Scheme (TDS), also contributed to the team’s scoring efforts and midfield structure during the competition.
His involvement is significant given the importance of structured talent identification and development programmes in building a pathway from grassroots football to the national teams.
Together, the players represent different parts of Nigeria’s football development landscape, from private academies to the NFF’s organised talent development structure.
Their participation in the festival provides an opportunity to assess their strengths, identify areas for improvement and determine how best to support their progress.
Nigeria has a long history of producing talented young footballers, with the country’s youth teams serving as an important pathway to the senior national side.
However, success at under-age level does not automatically guarantee a successful professional career. Many promising youngsters require years of consistent coaching, competitive exposure, education and appropriate welfare support before they can make the transition to elite football.
The performances in Baku therefore present both an opportunity and a responsibility for the NFF, the players’ academies and other stakeholders involved in youth development.
Ijachi’s 11 goals and three assists provide an impressive statistical foundation, but his next steps will be just as important as his exploits at the festival.
Regular competitive football, access to quality coaching, sound injury management and a carefully planned development pathway will be essential to ensure that his current promise translates into long-term progress.
The same applies to Oche, Muhammad, Boniface and Salu, whose performances have given Nigerian supporters additional reasons to follow the progress of the Future Eagles.
For the academies involved, the festival offers an opportunity to evaluate their development work against an international backdrop and identify areas where their players can improve technically, tactically and physically.
For the NFF, it reinforces the need to maintain a clear pathway for promising youngsters, ensuring that identification at under-15 level is followed by appropriate monitoring and opportunities to progress through the national youth teams.
The emphasis must be on building players for the future rather than judging their prospects solely on their performances in a single tournament.
As the maiden FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival approaches its conclusion in Baku, Ijachi stands out as one of Nigeria’s leading individual performers, while his teammates have demonstrated that the country has other emerging talents worth watching.
His 11 goals and three assists may have made him the name most likely to attract attention from Nigerian football followers, but the wider significance of the tournament lies in what comes next.
